Proyecto nuevo – Datos de préstamos e hipotecas (Prosper)¶

by José Luis Lázaro Contreras¶

Introduction¶

This project explores the Prosper Loan dataset, which contains detailed information about personal loans originated through the Prosper lending platform. The dataset includes borrower demographics, credit history, loan characteristics, and loan performance outcomes.

Given the size and richness of the dataset, this exploratory analysis focuses on understanding how borrower risk and loan characteristics relate to loan outcomes, particularly loan status and interest rates.

Objective of the analysis (solid proposal):

Analyze which factors are associated with the loan status (LoanStatus) and the borrower’s risk, focusing on variables such as:

interest rate / APR credit rating (ProsperRating, ProsperScore) income debt-to-income ratio (DTI) credit history

What is the structure of your dataset?¶

The Prosper Loan dataset is a large, loan-level dataset where each row represents a single loan originated on the Prosper platform. The dataset contains a substantial number of observations and a wide range of variables describing loan characteristics, borrower information, credit history, and loan performance outcomes.

The variables include a mix of numerical, categorical, and date-based fields. Key categories of information include loan status and amount, interest rates and APR, borrower income and employment details, credit scores and ratings, debt-related metrics, and historical loan performance indicators.

Due to the dataset’s size and complexity, a tolerant loading strategy was used to handle malformed records. Overall, the structure of the dataset is well suited for exploratory analysis at the univariate, bivariate, and multivariate levels, particularly for investigating factors related to borrower risk and loan outcomes.

What is/are the main feature(s) of interest in your dataset?¶

The main feature of interest in this dataset is the loan outcome, represented by the variable LoanStatus, which describes the current state of each loan (e.g., Current, Completed, Defaulted, or Chargedoff). This feature is central to understanding loan performance and borrower risk.

In addition, variables related to the cost of borrowing and risk assessment, such as Borrower APR (BorrowerAPR), interest rate (BorrowerRate), and Prosper risk ratings (e.g., ProsperRating (Alpha) and ProsperScore), are also key features of interest. These variables help explain how borrower risk is assessed and how it translates into loan pricing.

Together, these features allow the analysis to focus on how borrower characteristics and credit risk relate to loan outcomes and interest rates within the Prosper lending platform. ``

What features in the dataset do you think will help support your investigation into your feature(s) of interest¶

Several features in the dataset will help support the investigation into loan outcomes (LoanStatus) and borrower risk. Variables related to borrower creditworthiness are particularly important, including Prosper risk ratings such as ProsperRating (Alpha) and ProsperScore, as well as credit score ranges (CreditScoreRangeLower and CreditScoreRangeUpper). These features provide direct measures of borrower risk at the time the loan was originated.

Financial variables describing the borrower’s situation, such as debt-to-income ratio (DebtToIncomeRatio), stated income (StatedMonthlyIncome), and income range (IncomeRange), will also help explain differences in loan performance and pricing. These variables offer insight into a borrower’s ability to repay a loan.

Additional loan-related characteristics, including loan amount (LoanOriginalAmount), loan term (Term), and interest-related variables (BorrowerAPR and BorrowerRate), will support the analysis by showing how borrower risk translates into loan structure and cost.

Taken together, these features allow for a comprehensive exploration of how borrower characteristics and credit risk assessments are associated with loan outcomes and borrowing costs on the Prosper platform.

Univariate Exploration¶

In this section, individual variables are explored to understand their distributions and identify potential outliers or unusual patterns. This step helps establish a solid foundation for analyzing relationships between variables in later sections.

The exploration follows a logical progression:

  1. Loan outcome distribution
  2. Key risk and pricing variables
  3. Borrower financial characteristics

Observations¶

Most loans are either Current or Completed, indicating that the majority of loans are performing as expected. However, a noticeable number of loans fall into Chargedoff or Defaulted categories, highlighting the importance of understanding borrower risk factors and loan pricing.

Observations¶

The distribution of Borrower APR is right-skewed, with most loans concentrated at lower interest rates and a long tail extending toward higher APR values. This suggests that while many borrowers receive relatively affordable rates, a subset of higher-risk borrowers face significantly higher borrowing costs.

Discuss the distribution(s) of your variable(s) of interest. Were there any unusual points? Did you need to perform any transformations?¶

The main features of interest in this dataset are related to loan outcomes and risk/cost of borrowing, particularly LoanStatus, BorrowerAPR / BorrowerRate, and Prosper’s risk measures such as ProsperScore and ProsperRating (Alpha).

LoanStatus (loan outcome) is a categorical variable with multiple categories (e.g., Current, Completed, Chargedoff, Defaulted, PastDue). In the univariate exploration, the distribution shows that a large share of loans fall into “Current” and “Completed”, while a smaller but important portion are in negative outcome categories (e.g., “Chargedoff” or “Defaulted”). This imbalance is expected in loan performance data and motivates focusing on how borrower risk variables relate to these outcomes.

For the pricing variables, BorrowerAPR and BorrowerRate show distributions that are typically right-skewed, with most loans concentrated at lower-to-moderate rates and a tail of higher-cost loans. This tail represents borrowers with higher perceived risk paying substantially higher borrowing costs.

Risk indicators such as ProsperScore (1–10, with higher values indicating lower risk) and ProsperRating (categorical rating from higher-risk to lower-risk tiers) tend to cluster in mid-to-higher ranges, suggesting many loans were originated for borrowers with moderate to good credit profiles. These distributions are useful because they provide a direct, interpretable risk segmentation for later comparisons with loan outcomes and pricing.

Regarding unusual points, the most notable issues were related to data formatting and extreme values. Some numeric-looking fields (e.g., DebtToIncomeRatio) were loaded as strings due to non-standard formatting in the raw CSV and required conversion to numeric values using pd.to_numeric(..., errors='coerce'). In addition, variables with long right tails (like APR/rates or DTI) can be difficult to interpret on the original scale; therefore, range restrictions (for visualization clarity) and in some cases a log transformation were used to reduce skewness and better highlight the central distribution. These transformations were applied to improve interpretability rather than to remove information from the dataset.

Of the features you investigated, were there any unusual distributions? Did you perform any operations on the data to tidy, adjust, or change the form of the data? If so, why did you do this?¶

Yes, several features investigated during the univariate exploration displayed unusual distributions or data quality issues that required additional attention. One of the most notable cases was Debt-to-Income Ratio (DebtToIncomeRatio), which exhibited a strongly right-skewed distribution and contained extreme values. These extreme values made it difficult to interpret the distribution on the original scale.

To address this, two main adjustments were performed. First, the variable was converted from string to numeric format using pd.to_numeric(..., errors='coerce'), as some non-numeric or improperly formatted values were present in the raw dataset. Converting these values allowed invalid entries to be treated as missing rather than causing errors in analysis. Second, for visualization purposes, a range restriction and, in some cases, a log transformation were applied. These transformations helped reduce skewness and made the central tendency and overall shape of the distribution easier to interpret.

Similarly, pricing-related variables such as Borrower APR (BorrowerAPR) and Borrower Rate (BorrowerRate) showed right-skewed distributions with long tails toward higher values. While no data was removed, limiting the displayed range in visualizations helped prevent extreme values from dominating the plots and obscuring typical borrower behavior.

Categorical variables such as LoanStatus and ProsperScore did not display unusual distributions in a technical sense, but the strong imbalance across categories (e.g., many loans being “Current” or “Completed”) was noted. This imbalance is expected in loan performance data and was retained, as it reflects real-world outcomes rather than data quality problems.

Overall, the adjustments made during univariate exploration were lightweight and exploratory, focused on improving interpretability rather than altering the underlying data. These steps prepared the dataset for clearer bivariate and multivariate analysis without compromising the integrity of the original information.

Bivariate Exploration¶

In this section, relationships between pairs of variables are explored to understand how borrower risk characteristics and financial features relate to loan outcomes and pricing. The analysis builds directly on insights from the univariate exploration.

Scatter plot¶

Borrower APR vs Prosper Score

❓ Question,

How does borrower risk (Prosper Score) relate to the cost of borrowing (Borrower APR)?

In [29]:
# Ensure numeric
df_loans['CreditScoreRangeLower'] = pd.to_numeric(
    df_loans['CreditScoreRangeLower'], errors='coerce'
)

scatter_df = df_loans[['CreditScoreRangeLower', 'BorrowerAPR']].dropna()

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
sns.scatterplot(
    data=scatter_df,
    x='CreditScoreRangeLower',
    y='BorrowerAPR',
    alpha=0.3
)

plt.title('Borrower APR vs Lower Credit Score Range')
plt.xlabel('Credit Score (Lower Bound)')
plt.ylabel('Borrower APR')
plt.show()

Observations¶

A clear inverse relationship is observed between borrower credit score and Borrower APR. Loans issued to borrowers with lower credit scores tend to have higher APRs, indicating higher borrowing costs associated with increased credit risk.

Discussion of Bivariate Relationships¶

Several meaningful relationships were observed during the bivariate exploration, particularly involving the main features of interest related to loan outcomes and borrowing costs.

One of the clearest relationships appears between borrower credit risk measures and Borrower APR. Using credit score ranges as a proxy for borrower risk, loans issued to borrowers with lower credit scores are associated with higher APR values. This inverse relationship indicates that borrowers perceived as higher risk face higher borrowing costs, which aligns with standard credit pricing practices.

When examining Borrower APR across different loan outcomes (LoanStatus), loans that resulted in negative outcomes such as Chargedoff or Defaulted generally exhibit higher median APRs than loans that were Completed. This suggests that higher-cost loans are more likely to be associated with borrowers who ultimately experience repayment difficulties.

Grouped count and bar chart analyses further reinforce these findings. Loans classified into lower credit rating categories show a greater concentration of negative outcomes, while higher credit-quality loans are more frequently Current or Completed. Together, these patterns suggest a consistent link between borrower risk assessment, loan pricing, and loan performance.

Overall, the bivariate analysis demonstrates that borrower risk indicators and pricing variables vary systematically with loan outcomes. Borrower APR serves as an effective bridge between risk metrics and loan performance, providing a strong foundation for deeper multivariate exploration.

Did you observe any interesting relationships between the other features (not the main feature(s) of interest)?¶

Yes, a few interesting relationships emerged among features that were not the primary focus of the investigation. First, borrower financial characteristics such as IncomeRange / StatedMonthlyIncome and DebtToIncomeRatio appear to provide additional context about borrower affordability. While these variables were not used as the main feature(s) of interest, their distributions and group comparisons suggest that borrowers with higher income ranges often show different borrowing patterns compared to lower income ranges (e.g., differences in typical loan amounts or repayment structure).

Second, loan configuration variables such as loan term (Term) and loan size >(LoanOriginalAmount) can show meaningful variation across borrower groups. For example, longer terms tend to be associated with different monthly payment structures and may be more common in certain borrower profiles. These patterns are useful because they help explain how loans are structured, even before focusing directly on outcomes or APR.

Finally, it was noteworthy that some risk-related fields (such as ProsperScore) may not be populated in certain dataset versions or time periods. This limitation highlights the importance of relying on alternative risk proxies (e.g., credit score ranges or rating categories) when exploring relationships in the data. Recognizing which features are missing or only applicable to subsets of loans is an important part of interpreting secondary relationships accurately.

Multivariate Exploration¶

Prerequisite: Execute this cell once before the multivariate plots (converts to numeric and filters the basics).

In [32]:
# 0) Convert to numeric (avoids issues with string-type columns)
to_num = ['BorrowerAPR', 'BorrowerRate', 'LoanOriginalAmount',
          'DebtToIncomeRatio', 'CreditScoreRangeLower', 'CreditScoreRangeUpper']

for c in to_num:
    if c in df_loans.columns:
        df_loans[c] = pd.to_numeric(df_loans[c], errors='coerce')

# 1) Base subset (avoids NaN and impossible values)
mv_df = df_loans[['LoanStatus', 'BorrowerAPR', 'CreditScoreRangeLower',
                  'LoanOriginalAmount', 'Term', 'IncomeRange', 'DebtToIncomeRatio']].copy()

mv_df = mv_df.dropna(subset=['LoanStatus', 'BorrowerAPR', 'CreditScoreRangeLower', 'Term'])

# 2)Limit APR to a reasonable range (only for visualization; does not "delete" data from the original dataset)
mv_df = mv_df[(mv_df['BorrowerAPR'] >= 0) & (mv_df['BorrowerAPR'] <= 0.6)]

Faceted plot¶

Facet: relationship between "risk (score)" vs "APR" separated by loan status

Does the relationship between risk (credit score) and APR change depending on the loan status (LoanStatus)?

In [35]:
## Visualización (FacetGrid)
top_status = mv_df['LoanStatus'].value_counts().head(4).index
facet_df = mv_df[mv_df['LoanStatus'].isin(top_status)]

g = sns.FacetGrid(
    facet_df,
    col='LoanStatus',
    col_wrap=2,
    height=4,
    sharex=True,
    sharey=True
)

g.map_dataframe(
    sns.scatterplot,
    x='CreditScoreRangeLower',
    y='BorrowerAPR',
    alpha=0.25
)

# Add mean APR line per panel (relevant annotation)
def add_mean_line(data, **kws):
    mean_apr = data['BorrowerAPR'].mean()
    plt.axhline(mean_apr, color='red', linestyle='--', linewidth=1)

g.map_dataframe(add_mean_line)

g.set_axis_labels('Credit Score (Lower Bound)', 'Borrower APR')
g.set_titles('{col_name}')
g.fig.suptitle('Borrower APR vs Credit Score by Loan Status', y=1.05)

plt.show()

plt.ylabel('Mean Borrower APR')
plt.legend(title='Loan Status', bbox_to_anchor=(1.05, 1), loc='upper left')
plt.show()

Observations¶

Average APR varies by both term and loan status. The overall mean line helps contextualize which groups are above or below typical pricing. This suggests that loan configuration (term length) interacts with outcome categories in loan pricing patterns.

Conclusions¶

This exploratory analysis examined the Prosper Loan dataset with the goal of understanding how borrower risk, loan characteristics, and pricing relate to loan outcomes. By progressing systematically through univariate, bivariate, and multivariate exploration, several key findings and methodological insights emerged.

Summary of Main Findings¶

  • Loan outcomes are highly imbalanced, with most loans classified as Current or Completed, while a smaller but meaningful portion results in negative outcomes such as Chargedoff or Defaulted. This imbalance reflects real-world lending behavior and motivates a focus on borrower risk factors.
  • Borrower APR is strongly associated with borrower risk measures. Higher borrowing costs are consistently observed for borrowers with lower credit scores or weaker risk indicators, confirming that loan pricing reflects perceived credit risk.
  • Credit score ranges and rating categories provide useful proxies for borrower risk, particularly when other risk variables (such as ProsperScore) are unavailable in certain dataset versions.
  • Higher APRs are more common among loans with negative outcomes, suggesting that borrowers who are riskier at origination—and therefore face higher interest rates—are also more likely to experience repayment difficulties.
